title: Bloomberg New Economy Forum: Higher Yields Doing Some of the Work
summary: In a moderated conversation in New Delhi dominated by AI, fiscal risk and Fed independence, Waller does not repeat the explicit call he made in Istanbul on October 8 ('I anticipate additional hikes'). Asked directly whether the surge in long yields is enough or whether the Fed has more room to hike, he sidesteps the path and says the ten-year is set by global supply and demand, but that higher yields hit housing and autos and are 'doing a little bit of the work', a new argument that partially substitutes for policy-rate tightening. He keeps an inflation-side worry: the AI buildout is 'spreading out' inflation through demand for chips and related goods and could last 2 to 3 years, and 'we have to just decide how we want to respond to that', though he calls the effect narrow rather than broad-based and stresses that inflation expectations are well anchored, softening his Istanbul concern about expectations drifting up. The rest covers the fading Treasury convenience yield, fiscal dominance (not yet a US problem) and defending Fed independence; labor is not discussed. The score falls versus Istanbul because of the format and the financial-conditions offset, not because of an explicit retreat on hikes.

key_quotes.quote: So it's doing a little bit of the work.
key_quotes.context: Answering whether higher long yields are enough or the Fed has more room to hike: higher yields tighten demand in housing and autos, a spillover that is not the Fed's intent.

key_quotes.quote: we're starting to see AI having a spreading out of inflation, because it's just increasing demand for everything else.
key_quotes.context: Hyperscalers bidding up semiconductor prices; he sees the pressure lasting 2 to 3 years.

key_quotes.quote: And we have to just decide how we want to respond to that.
key_quotes.context: After saying hyperscalers plan to keep spending trillions over three years, so the AI demand pressure may persist.
Explaining that the rise in yields reflects real growth and fiscal concerns, not an inflation premium.
